title: Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States
court: United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit
subject: Substantial Rights / Funded Research
summary: Lockheed Martin v. United States (Fed. Cir. 2000) is a landmark federal R&D tax credit case for U.S. contractors performing research under fixed-price agreements. The Federal Circuit held that a non-exclusive right to use research results without paying for that right is a "substantial right" defeating the funded research exclusion, but barred refund claims from adding newly discovered expenses.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Taxpayer's Claim and Factual Context

In Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. 2000), the plaintiff-appellant, Lockheed Martin Corporation—acting as the successor in interest to Martin Marietta Corporation, Martin Marietta Technologies, Inc., and affiliated subsidiary corporations—sought a federal income tax refund of research and experimentation (R&E) tax credits based on research expenses incurred from 1982 through 1988 (the opinion does not state the total dollar amount of the refund claimed). During the 1982 through 1988 tax years, the taxpayer was a party to numerous fixed-price contracts with the United States, including Department of Defense programs, to design, develop, test, and manufacture advanced defense and aerospace systems.

The research credits at issue were sought through amended returns rather than the original returns: in 1991, the taxpayer filed administrative claims for refund (Forms 1120X) for the 1984 through 1988 tax years, based on research expenses incurred from 1982 to 1988 in the performance of the fixed-price contracts. The refund claims asserted entitlement to the credit for increasing research activities based on qualified research expenses (QREs) incurred pursuant to fixed-price customer contracts where the right to payment was contingent upon the success of the research (citing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1)), as well as additionally qualifying wages for holiday, vacation, sick, military-leave, and jury-duty pay that had been inadvertently omitted.

Attached to each administrative refund claim was a Form 6765 stating the amounts spent by category of research expense, together with a high-level summary schedule apportioning those amounts across the taxpayer's corporate divisions; for example, the $16,540,427 of 1986 research supply costs was allocated $16,472,519 to Martin Marietta Corporation, $62,900 to Martin Marietta Information Technology, Inc., $5,008 to Martin Marietta Measurement Systems, Inc., and $0 to both Martin Marietta Aluminum Properties, Inc. and Gamma Monolithics Partnership. However, the taxpayer did not submit contemporaneous documentary evidence or contract-level accounting schedules with the initial refund forms. Instead, when the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) initiated its administrative examination of the refund claims, the taxpayer produced schedules of specific expenses incurred in performing the 13 largest contracts underlying its refund claims—referred to by both parties as the "Green Books"—which covered approximately 80 percent of the total expenses underlying the refund claims. After the IRS disallowed the claims and the taxpayer sued in the United States Court of Federal Claims, the parties agreed to resolve the "substantial rights" issue on cross-motions for summary judgment by reference to the contracts governing four programs representing approximately 65 percent of the expenses claimed—the Low Altitude Navigation and Targeting InfraRed for Night (LANTIRN), Small Intercontinental Ballistic Missile (SICBM or "Midgetman"), Supersonic Low Altitude Target (SLAT), and Titan IV programs, designated the "Major Programs"—and to extend the result, pro rata, to all contracts in the suit. During discovery on the LANTIRN contract, the taxpayer learned of additional research expenses that it had not included in its Green Books, prompting it to file a "motion for pretrial order clarifying the scope of complaint" asking the court to order the government to consider evidence of these expenses and any others uncovered in discovery.
The Tax Authority's Challenge

The IRS had disallowed the refund claims on the ground that the research was "funded" under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d) because payment was not contingent on the success of the research and Lockheed Martin did not retain substantial rights in the research. In the litigation, the United States, represented by the Department of Justice Tax Division, mounted a bifurcated challenge targeting both the jurisdictional scope of the taxpayer's evidentiary submission and the substantive eligibility of the underlying contract research. On the procedural front, the government opposed the taxpayer's motion to introduce the post-complaint QREs, invoking the doctrine of "substantial variance" under Internal Revenue Code (I.R.C.) § 7422(a) and Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1). The government contended that, although the claims were written broadly, they were predicated on specific expenses that formed their factual basis; that later-discovered expenses by definition could not constitute the factual predicate for an earlier claim; and that the taxpayer had represented that the Green Books contained all of the expenses on which its claims for the 13 contracts were predicated, so that introducing newly discovered cost items would impermissibly vary the factual basis of the claims.

On the substantive front, both parties moved for summary judgment, with the government contending that all research expenditures incurred under the Major Program contracts were statutorily disqualified as "funded research" under I.R.C. § 44F(d)(3) and § 41(d)(4)(H). Relying on Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d) (subsequently redesignated as Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3), the government argued that even if a contractor bears financial risk under a fixed-price agreement, the research is treated as fully funded if the taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the research under the agreement providing for the research. The government conceded that Lockheed Martin retained the right to use and disclose the results of its research, but argued that this right was not "substantial" because the contracts' recoupment provision required Lockheed Martin to pay to use the research, because the government had the right to use the technical data and computer software and disclose them to third parties (and to use or sell any patented invention) without Lockheed Martin being able to prevent it, and because top secret security provisions and export control laws further restricted sales of products resulting from the research. Consequently, the government argued that Lockheed Martin's rights to use and disclose its research had "no practical value"; it was the Court of Federal Claims that went on to characterize the profits Lockheed Martin received on private sales of related technology as "incidental benefits".
Governing Statutory and Regulatory Framework

The dispute spanned two statutory iterations of the federal research credit within the Internal Revenue Code of 1954 and the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. For the earlier tax years at issue, I.R.C. § 44F(a), originally enacted by the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 to incentivize private-sector research investment, allowed a tax credit equal to 25 percent of the excess of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses for the taxable year over its base period research expenses. The Tax Reform Act of 1984 renumbered § 44F as § 30, and the Tax Reform Act of 1986 (TRA 86) renumbered § 30 as § 41 and substantially amended it; I.R.C. § 41(a), which similarly provided an incremental credit equal to 20 percent of the excess of qualified research expenses over a statutory base amount, before being made permanent in 2015.

Both I.R.C. § 44F(d) and § 41(d) linked the foundational definition of "qualified research" to "research or experimental" expenditures under I.R.C. § 174, while carving out express statutory exclusions for research conducted outside the United States, research in the social sciences or humanities, and funded research. Central to this litigation was the "funded research" exclusion codified at I.R.C. § 44F(d)(3) and carried forward in substantially similar form into I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H), which excludes from qualified research any research to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person or any governmental entity.

Because the statutory text did not define the term "funded" or reference intellectual property ownership, the governing analytical framework derived from the Treasury Regulations promulgated under Section 41—specifically Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d), which was finalized in T.D. 8251 in 1989 and later redesignated in T.D. 8930 as Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) via the cross-reference in Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(c)(9), alongside the "trade or business" regulations at Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3). These regulations establish a conjunctive, two-pronged regime for evaluating research performed for third parties. Under the first prong governing financial risk allocation, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(1)) provides that research is not considered funded to the extent that amounts payable under the agreement are contingent on the success of the research. Such contingent payments are treated under the regulatory "mirror rules" as consideration paid for the product or result of the research rather than funding for the performance of the research itself, thereby allocating the tax credit to the party bearing the financial risk of technical failure.

Under the second prong governing the retention of substantial rights, even where payment is contingent on technical success, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(2) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(2)) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3)(i) mandate that if a taxpayer performing research for another person retains no substantial rights in research under the agreement providing for the research, the research is treated as fully funded, and no expenses paid or incurred by the researcher qualify for the credit. Crucially, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(3)(i) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)) stipulates that a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research. Furthermore, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(2) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(2)) provides that incidental benefits to the taxpayer from performance of the research, such as increased experience in a field of research, do not constitute substantial rights in the research. Procedurally, the litigation was governed by I.R.C. § 7422(a), which bars any civil suit for the recovery of internal revenue taxes until a claim for refund has been duly filed according to Treasury regulations, and Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), which mandates that the administrative claim set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof.
The Court's Final Holding

The litigation produced two published trial court opinions in the United States Court of Federal Claims—Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 39 Fed. Cl. 197 (1997) addressing claim variance, and Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 42 Fed. Cl. 485 (1998) addressing substantial rights—both decided against the taxpayer; the appeal was taken from Judge Diane Gilbert Weinstein of that court. On appeal, a unanimous panel of the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, in an opinion authored by Circuit Judge Alan D. Lourie and joined by Circuit Judges Plager and Bryson, issued a landmark decision on April 26, 2000, that affirmed-in-part, reversed-in-part, and remanded the case.

On the procedural issue of substantial variance, the Federal Circuit affirmed the trial court's denial of the taxpayer's motion to introduce newly discovered QREs. The appellate court held that, although the claims were written broadly, each was based on a finite group of expenses that constituted its factual basis even though the details were not provided to the IRS; expenses not discovered until after suit was filed were not among the expenses on which the claims were predicated, so introducing them would constitute a substantial variance of the factual basis of the claims, barred by I.R.C. § 7422(a) and Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1). On the substantive issue of substantial rights and funded research, the Federal Circuit reversed the trial court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the government and held that summary judgment should have been granted in favor of Lockheed Martin because, having retained substantial rights, its research under the Major Program contracts did not fall under the "funded" exclusion. Rejecting the trial court's reliance on patent assignment jurisprudence, the Federal Circuit established the controlling federal standard that the right to use the research results in the taxpayer's trade or business without paying for that right, even if non-exclusive, is a "substantial right" under the Treasury Regulations. The court further held that substantial rights must be determined by reference to the Major Program contracts alone, so that export control laws and top secret security classifications—which lie outside the research agreements—are irrelevant, and that contractual cost recoupment clauses triggered only upon commercial third-party sales do not restrict the contractor's right to make and use the research results internally. The case was remanded to the Court of Federal Claims "for further proceedings consistent with this opinion"; the opinion noted that whether the research was funded because payment was not contingent on success had not been raised on appeal, and that it was unclear from the briefs whether the government had conceded that issue or withdrawn it as a ground for disallowance.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

The Lockheed Martin litigation exposes two distinct categories of vulnerabilities in federal R&D tax credit practice: first, the actual evidentiary and procedural failures committed by the taxpayer during the preparation of its administrative refund claims, which permanently forfeited additional, otherwise potentially qualifying research expenses under the substantial variance doctrine; and second, the contractual and interpretive vulnerabilities surrounding intellectual property, regulatory restrictions, and payment contingency, which caused the IRS and the Court of Federal Claims to disqualify the entire claim at the trial level and which continue to govern contract research disputes in the United States Tax Court and federal appellate courts today.
Administrative Claim Deficiencies, Post-Filing Accounting, and the Substantial Variance Doctrine

The taxpayer's sole defeat at the Federal Circuit stemmed from a classic operational failure in corporate R&D tax credit administration: filing protective or loosely substantiated refund claims before completing a bottom-up, project-by-project accounting of all qualifying expenditures. When the taxpayer filed its Forms 1120X for the 1984–1988 tax years, it articulated a clear legal ground—that research expenses incurred under fixed-price contracts where payment was contingent on research success were qualified under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1)—and attached top-level summary sheets allocating total dollar figures across corporate entities. However, the taxpayer did not submit the underlying factual evidence until the IRS audit commenced, at which point it provided the Green Books detailing the specific costs by contract.

During discovery on the LANTIRN contract after filing suit in the Court of Federal Claims, the taxpayer learned of additional research expenses that it had not included in its Green Books. The taxpayer argued that the legal basis, the class of contract, and the categories of expenses underlying its claims remained unchanged, that its broadly written claims put the government on notice that it sought credits for wages, supplies, contract research, and rent expenses under its fixed-price contracts, and that the Green Books were merely evidence for proving its claims rather than the claims themselves.

Both the Court of Federal Claims (39 Fed. Cl. 197) and the Federal Circuit rejected this argument, enforcing the filing prerequisite of I.R.C. § 7422(a) and Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1). As the Federal Circuit explained, the substantial variance rule contains two independent components: a legal component, which prohibits any legal theory not expressly or impliedly contained in the application for refund, and a factual component, which requires the taxpayer to set forth facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis of the claim. The Court of Federal Claims reasoned that the additional expenses could have constituted a separate basis for recovery had they been timely filed; the Federal Circuit added that each refund claim was based on a finite group of expenses that the taxpayer summed to arrive at its credit, that those expenses constituted the factual basis of the claim even though their details were not provided to the IRS, and that expenses discovered after suit was filed—several years after the claims—were not among them. The court explained that the substantial variance rule gives the IRS notice of the nature of the claim and the specific facts on which it is predicated, gives the IRS an opportunity to correct errors, and limits litigation to grounds the IRS had an opportunity to consider and is willing to defend.

The broader implication for corporate tax departments is severe. Even when a taxpayer files an administrative refund claim with only high-level summary schedules, the factual basis of the claim is the finite set of expenses on which it was actually predicated, and the court observed that had the taxpayer submitted a detailed listing of expenses with its claim, there would be no dispute that it could not vary from that list. Any QREs that were not among the expenses underlying the claim—for example, because of decentralized enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, incomplete cost-center mapping, or rushed pre-filing sampling—cannot be introduced in the refund suit unless the claim is amended to include them within the limitations period.
Contractual IP Allocation and the "Substantial Rights" Misconception

On the substantive merits, the dispute centered on how contractual intellectual property (IP) clauses in complex engineering contracts interact with the "substantial rights" requirement of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(2) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(2)) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3). Under the Major Program contracts, standard regulatory clauses incorporated by reference (from the Defense Acquisition Regulation and the FAR/DFARS) governed the allocation of patent rights and technical data, and the contracts also contained security classification guidelines. Specifically, the "Patent Rights Clause — Retention by the Contractor" in the Titan IV, LANTIRN FSED, and SLAT contracts (with a substantially similar clause in the SICBM contract, and no patent clause in the LANTIRN Production contract) provided that the contractor may retain the entire right, title, and interest throughout the world or any country thereof in and to each Subject Invention disclosed, subject to granting the U.S. Government a nonexclusive, nontransferable, paid-up license to make, use, and sell each Subject Invention throughout the world. With respect to technical data and computer software, the government acquired the unlimited right to use, duplicate, and disclose to others a wide range of technical data, software, databases, and other information developed under the contract, and the right to permit others to do so, but the clause did not restrict Lockheed Martin's own right to use or disclose that information.

In disqualifying the taxpayer's claim, the Court of Federal Claims (42 Fed. Cl. 485) relied in part on an analogy to the "all substantial rights" concept from federal patent jurisprudence—specifically Vaupel Textilmaschinen KG v. Meccanica Euro Italia S.P.A., 944 F.2d 870 (Fed. Cir. 1991)—in construing the tax regulations. In patent law, courts examine whether a transferor has conveyed "all substantial rights" in a patent to determine whether an agreement constitutes a complete assignment (conferring standing to sue for infringement) rather than a mere license. The trial court concluded that Lockheed Martin did not retain substantial rights because (1) the government's unlimited right to use the technical data and disclose it to third parties "considerably diminished, if not destroyed" the value of Lockheed Martin's right to use its research and its competitive advantage; (2) Lockheed Martin had to obtain prior State Department approval before entering into licensing agreements or discussing non-public technical information with other customers; (3) the government had veto power over Lockheed Martin's patent filings and could require transfer of title to a subject invention if no application was filed in time; and (4) the recoupment provision required Lockheed Martin to pay for the right to use its research results.

Writing for the Federal Circuit, Judge Lourie dismantled this analogy as legally unsound. The court observed that the patent cases deal with whether all substantial rights have been transferred so as to make an agreement an assignment rather than a license, whereas the tax statute and regulations, with different language and concepts, do not require the retention of all substantial rights; the regulation asks whether the taxpayer retains no substantial rights. Nothing in I.R.C. § 41 or the Treasury Regulations requires a researcher to retain exclusive ownership or the right to exclude others. Instead, reading Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d) alongside Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a), the Federal Circuit held that the right to use the research results, even without the exclusive right, is a substantial right. Because the patent clauses left rights to all patents and inventions with Lockheed Martin (subject only to the government's nonexclusive, nontransferable, paid-up license), and because the government conceded that the contract provisions gave Lockheed Martin the right to use its research in its business—a right the court called "clearly substantial" because it permits Lockheed Martin to manufacture and sell up-to-date products—the taxpayer satisfied the substantial rights test as a matter of law.

However, the Federal Circuit's opinion established a strict interpretive rule that has subsequently proved fatal to poorly drafted commercial contracts: whether a taxpayer retains substantial rights must be determined strictly by reference to the research agreements executed by the parties. In the decades following Lockheed Martin, the IRS and the United States Tax Court have enforced this "four corners of the agreement" rule against custom manufacturers, software developers, and architectural and engineering firms. As demonstrated in Tangel v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-1, and Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, when a contractor signs a commercial agreement containing a broad boilerplate non-disclosure or IP clause prohibiting the contractor from disclosing, reproducing, or using the technical specifications, designs, or data developed under the contract without the client's prior written consent, the contractor retains "no substantial rights" under the agreement. Contrastingly, where architectural or engineering contracts vest copyright ownership of final construction documents in the client but contain no provision prohibiting the researcher from reusing the underlying research results without paying the client—as in Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Docket No. 405-17 (2019)—the Tax Court applies Lockheed Martin to hold that substantial rights are retained.
Cost Recoupment Clauses, Sovereign Export Controls (ITAR), and the "Incidental Benefits" Trap

Two additional contractual and regulatory facets of the Major Program contracts formed the centerpiece of the government's challenge: cost recoupment provisions and statutory export controls. The Major Program contracts incorporated a "Recovery of Nonrecurring Costs on Commercial Sales" clause requiring Lockheed Martin, when it entered into domestic or foreign commercial sales of contract items or essentially similar items, or licensed technology developed under the contract, to reimburse the U.S. Government a fair share of its nonrecurring costs (or, for technology, the government's proportionate share of the fair market price), generally where the government's investment equaled or exceeded $5 million. The government and the Court of Federal Claims relied upon this clause, contending that it triggered the disqualifying rule of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(3)(i) (now § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i)), which states that a taxpayer does not retain substantial rights in the research if the taxpayer must pay for the right to use the results of the research.

The Federal Circuit reversed, drawing a critical analytical distinction between paying to use research results in one's trade or business versus reimbursing development costs upon the commercial sale of a finished product or license. The appellate court characterized the clause as a cost-recovery provision, contrasting it with a payment for the right to use, which is generally a percentage or per-item royalty based on sales rather than a reimbursement of research and development costs. The clause applied only when Lockheed Martin intended to sell contract items or essentially similar items, or to sell or license related technology, to third parties. It did not restrict Lockheed Martin's right to make the subject products, essentially similar products, or related technology and use them in its own business, did not affect its right to make and use patented inventions or to exclude unauthorized third parties, and did not restrict its right to use the technical data and software—and even the right to sell was not precluded if reimbursement was made. Thus, a cost-reimbursement obligation triggered by commercial sales or licensing to third parties does not negate substantial rights where the contractor retains the right to use the research results in its business without paying for that right.

Furthermore, the trial court held that Lockheed Martin lacked substantial rights for the further reason that particular statutory provisions restricted its exports, and it relied on the requirement of prior State Department approval for licensing or for discussing non-public technical information with other customers. Separately, the trial court characterized the profits Lockheed Martin received on private sales of related technology as "incidental benefits".

The Federal Circuit rejected both points. It held that export control laws and top secret classifications are irrelevant to the inquiry because they are outside of the research agreements, and that the determination whether Lockheed Martin retained substantial rights must be made by reference to the Major Program contracts alone. Because the regulation focuses on the taxpayer's rights "under the agreement providing for the research," restrictions arising outside the research agreements cannot strip a taxpayer of substantial rights. Moreover, because the contracts gave Lockheed Martin the right to use its research results in its business without paying for that right, the court held that it retained substantial rights—rejecting the trial court's conclusion that those rights were "considerably diminished, if not destroyed"—whereas the regulation's example of a mere incidental benefit is increased experience in a field of research.
The Dual-Prong Funded Research Nexus: Contingency of Payment on Technical Success vs. General Economic Risk

A critical second-order consequence of Lockheed Martin is that prevailing on the "substantial rights" issue does not by itself establish entitlement to the R&D tax credit; rather, it simply clears one half of a mandatory two-part regulatory hurdle. In analyzing Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d), the Federal Circuit synthesized its prior decision in Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. 1995), with the substantial rights rule, confirming that a contractor's research is treated as "funded" under two independent scenarios: when the parties agree that payment shall not be contingent on the success of the research, or when the taxpayer retains no substantial rights in the research. In Lockheed Martin itself, however, the payment-contingency question was not raised on appeal—the court noted it was unclear whether the government had conceded that payment was contingent on success or had withdrawn that ground—so the court decided only the substantial rights issue, held that the research did not fall under the funded exclusion, and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

This conjunctive structure—requiring the taxpayer to prove both financial risk (payment contingent on research success) and substantial rights—has become the primary battleground in modern U.S. R&D tax credit litigation. Under the "mirror rule" architecture of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3) and § 1.41-4A(d), Congress and the Treasury sought to allocate the tax credit to the party bearing the financial risk of failed innovation. Yet, because the regulations impose the substantial rights requirement alongside the payment-contingency requirement, a harsh asymmetry emerges: if a custom developer incurs massive cost overruns on a fixed-price contract (bearing 100% of the economic risk) but fails to retain substantial rights in the contract boilerplate, the developer receives zero credit, and the customer (whose payments were contingent on success) cannot claim the payments as contract research expenses either. Even where a researcher's total research expenses exceed the funding received, the default allocation rule under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3) stacks funding first against otherwise creditable expenses, and denies any pro-rata allocation if the taxpayer retains no substantial rights. In 2026, in Smith v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-50, taxpayers challenged the validity of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d) following the Supreme Court's abrogation of Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), arguing that the statutory word "funded" in I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) looks solely to cash flow and does not authorize a "substantial rights" test. The Tax Court squarely rejected the Loper Bright challenge, citing Lockheed Martin to uphold the regulation's two-step framework.

Moreover, even when a taxpayer satisfies Lockheed Martin's substantial rights standard, courts in subsequent decisions—including Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015), Dynetics, Inc. v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015), United States v. Grigsby, 86 F.4th 602 (5th Cir. 2023), Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. (MBJ) v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. 2024), and Smith v. Commissioner (2026)—have strictly policed the first prong. These courts have established that fixed-price contracts are not per se unfunded. Bearing the "general economic risk" of investing labor and resources without a commitment to be paid, or suffering a cost overrun or loss of profit opportunity on a fixed-price services or design contract, is legally insufficient. To satisfy the Fairchild and Lockheed Martin payment-contingency standard, the contract must expressly or by clear implication condition the customer's obligation to pay—and the contractor's right to retain interim progress payments—upon the technical success of the research and the formal inspection, evaluation, testing, and acceptance of a research-driven deliverable against detailed technical performance specifications.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory, regulatory, and procedural requirement adjudicated in Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States against the specific evidentiary or contractual vulnerability identified in the dispute, the trial court's ruling, and the controlling standard of proof established by the Federal Circuit.

Reg. § 1.41-5(d) and § 1.41-2(a), exclusivity is not required; the non-exclusive right to use the research results in the taxpayer's trade or business without paying for that right is a "substantial right". Exclusion of Mere "Incidental Benefits" I.R.C. § 41(b)(1); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3)

Government argued that, given its rights in the technical data and inventions, the recoupment clause, and security and export restrictions, Lockheed Martin's conceded rights to use and disclose its research had "no practical value".
Ruled Against Taxpayer (42 Fed. Cl. 485): Characterized the taxpayer's profits from private sales of related technology as "incidental benefits," insufficient to confer substantial rights.

Reversed in Favor of Taxpayer: The regulation's example of an "incidental benefit" is increased experience in a field of research, which does not prevent research from being treated as funded where the taxpayer lacks the right to use the results. Because the contracts gave Lockheed Martin the right to use its research results in its business without paying for that right, it retained substantial rights.
Contingency of Payment on Technical Success (Financial Risk Allocation) I.R.C. § 41(d)(4)(H); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1) [now § 1.41-4A(d)(1)]

Taxpayer claimed QREs under fixed-price contracts, asserting that payment was contingent on the success of the research under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-5(d)(1); the IRS disallowed in part because it concluded payment was not contingent on success. Trial court decided the cross-motions for summary judgment on substantial rights.

Not Adjudicated / Bypassed on Summary Judgment (42 Fed. Cl. 485): Bypassed detailed payment-contingency analysis across all contracts by holding that lack of substantial rights alone rendered the research 100% funded.

Not Raised on Appeal; Remanded for Further Proceedings Consistent with the Opinion: Described the two scenarios in which research is "funded" under the regulation—payment not contingent on success (citing Fairchild), or no substantial rights retained—so that avoiding the exclusion requires both that payment be contingent on success and that substantial rights be retained. The court noted that payment contingency had not been raised on appeal and that it was unclear whether the government had conceded it or withdrawn it, reversed, held that summary judgment should have been granted in Lockheed Martin's favor, and remanded for further proceedings consistent with its opinion.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To translate the appellate holdings of Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States—and the subsequent jurisprudence applying its framework, including Fairchild, Geosyntec, Dynetics, Tangel, Grigsby, MBJ, and Smith—into actionable tax and legal practice, counsel must address project governance, contract drafting, risk engineering, and contemporaneous substantiation before contracts are executed and tax returns or refund claims are filed. The following two applied case studies demonstrate step-by-step how taxpayers in high-audit-risk industries can remediate the exact legal and evidentiary traps identified in the ruling.
Case Study 1: Aerospace & Defense Prime Contractor (Autonomous Hypersonic Flight Control System)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

Aegis AeroSystems Corp. ("Aegis"), a domestic Tier-1 aerospace and defense contractor, enters into a $140 million Fixed-Price Incentive (Firm Target) (FPIF) contract with the United States Air Force to design, develop, and qualify an autonomous thermal-protection and flight-control subsystem for a hypersonic glide vehicle. The project faces four acute vulnerabilities directly mirroring the disputes in Lockheed Martin and its progeny. First, regarding substantial variance risk under I.R.C. § 7422(a) and Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2, Aegis operates three decentralized engineering divisions across incompatible legacy ERP systems; its corporate tax department plans to file an amended return (Form 1120X) for an expiring tax year using top-level divisional estimates while deferring a detailed review of engineering supply accounts and subcontractor invoices until an IRS audit occurs. Second, regarding intellectual property and technical data restriction risk under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2), although the prime contract incorporates standard DFARS patent clauses, a Special Contract Requirement (Section H clause) drafted by the procuring program office states that all technical data, aerodynamic models, source code, and design documentation generated under the contract shall be the sole property of the Government, and prohibits Aegis from reproducing, disclosing, or utilizing any data or designs developed thereunder for any non-contract purpose without the prior written approval of the Contracting Officer. Third, regarding recoupment and export control confusion under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i), the contract includes a Special Defense Acquisition Fund recoupment clause requiring Aegis to pay a 7 percent recoupment charge on any non-U.S. Government sales of derivatives, and subjects all technical data to strict ITAR export controls and Secret-level security classification. Fourth, regarding payment-contingency vulnerability under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1), Aegis receives monthly progress payments under FAR 52.232-16 equal to 80 percent of its incurred costs based on routine monthly invoices, without tying each payment liquidation to a formal technical acceptance test.
Step 1: Project Governance & Pre-Claim Administrative Protocol (Overcoming the Substantial Variance Doctrine)

To prevent the permanent forfeiture of QREs experienced by Lockheed Martin in 39 Fed. Cl. 197 and 210 F.3d at 1371–72, Aegis must overhaul its tax compliance governance prior to filing Form 1120X. Corporate tax leadership must institute a strict governance mandate prohibiting the filing of any administrative refund claim based on placeholder figures or partial divisional summaries. Before the statute of limitations under I.R.C. § 6511 expires, Aegis must execute a unified cross-divisional data extraction across all three ERP systems, mapping every W-2 wage account, general ledger supply account (specifically capturing prototype materials charged to direct contract cost centers), and 65 percent contract research sub-account to specific Contract Line Item Numbers (CLINs).

In accordance with Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) and modern IRS administrative specificity standards, Aegis must compile its complete "Green Book" substantiation binder prior to submission and attach an exhaustive contract-by-contract breakdown directly to the Form 1120X. This submission must explicitly identify each business component (individual hypersonic flight-control hardware units and embedded flight software modules), detail the qualified research activities performed per business component, and state the exact dollar amount of qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses per business component. If any secondary division's cost accounting records remain under internal review when the initial Form 1120X is filed, tax counsel must calendar a mandatory cut-off date at least 90 days prior to the expiration of the I.R.C. § 6511 limitations period to file a formal supplemental Form 1120X incorporating any newly discovered QREs into the administrative record before the IRS issues a Notice of Disallowance or litigation is commenced.
Step 2: Contractual Restructuring & IP Carve-Outs (Satisfying the Substantial Rights Standard)

While the standard FAR and DFARS framework passed muster in Lockheed Martin, the bespoke Section H clause in Aegis's contract creates a fatal Tangel and Smith defect by requiring Contracting Officer approval before Aegis can use the research results for non-contract purposes. Aegis's legal and government contracts team must negotiate a bilateral contract modification (or structure initial Request for Proposal exceptions) to align the agreement with the Federal Circuit's holding. Specifically, Aegis must ensure the contract incorporates FAR 52.227-11 or DFARS 252.227-7038 (Patent Rights—Ownership by the Contractor), under which Aegis retains the entire right, title, and interest throughout the world to each Subject Invention, granting the U.S. Government only a non-exclusive, nontransferable, irrevocable, paid-up license to practice the invention for government purposes.

Crucially, Aegis must modify the bespoke Section H clause to delete the prior-consent restriction on internal research usage and distinguish between classified physical deliverables and underlying engineering research results. The amended Section H clause should explicitly state that notwithstanding the Government's Unlimited Rights in delivered Technical Data and Computer Software under DFARS 252.227-7013 and 252.227-7014, the Contractor retains the perpetual, non-exclusive, royalty-free right to make, use, reproduce, modify, and exploit all research results, engineering methodologies, thermodynamic models, algorithms, inventions, and technical know-how conceived, developed, or reduced to practice in the performance of the contract within the Contractor's internal research, development, manufacturing, and commercial or government trade or business, without any obligation to seek prior consent from, or pay any royalty or license fee to, the Government.

Furthermore, to ensure the 7 percent cost recoupment clause complies with Lockheed Martin, Aegis must draft the provision to specify that recoupment fees apply solely to the commercial sale or third-party licensing of the identical manufactured end-item (the specific military flight-control hardware unit), while expressly stating that nothing in the recoupment clause requires Aegis to pay any fee, royalty, or reimbursement to the Government for Aegis's internal use of the research results, technical data, or software in its trade or business, or in the design and development of distinct commercial or defense products. Finally, all references to ITAR (22 C.F.R. Parts 120–130), the Arms Export Control Act (22 U.S.C. § 2778), and DD Form 254 security classifications must be isolated in a separate "Regulatory Compliance" section stating that such restrictions are acknowledged solely as preexisting obligations of sovereign federal law and do not alter the contractual allocation of intellectual property or usage rights between the parties.
Step 3: Financial Risk & Payment Contingency Engineering (Satisfying the Remand Standard)

To defeat an IRS contention on audit or remand that monthly progress payments under FAR 52.232-16 render the research "funded", Aegis must structure the payment and inspection mechanics to mirror Fairchild Industries (71 F.3d 868). The contract must be divided into discrete, severable research and prototype CLINs tied to objective technical performance milestones, specifically Preliminary Design Review (PDR) wind-tunnel validation, Critical Design Review (CDR) thermal-structural qualification at Mach 6+ simulated environments, and Flight Readiness Qualification Testing.

The contract payment schedule must explicitly stipulate that all monthly progress payments under FAR 52.232-16 are strictly unliquidated financing advances rather than earned revenue. By integrating strict Inspection and Acceptance clauses (FAR 52.246-2 and FAR 52.246-8), the contract must provide that Aegis remains financially at risk for each CLIN until the research is successfully completed and the deliverable is formally accepted. If Aegis fails to resolve the technological uncertainties and the prototype fails to meet the contract's technical performance specifications during formal government acceptance testing, the Government holds the contractual right to reject the deliverable, require Aegis to re-engineer and cure the defective research at Aegis's sole financial expense without adjusting the ceiling price, or terminate the contract for default and demand 100 percent repayment of all unliquidated progress payments previously advanced for that CLIN.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Technical Documentation & Experimentation Tracking

To substantiate the four-part test of I.R.C. § 41(d) alongside the unfunded nature of the contract, Aegis must establish dedicated Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) charge codes prior to project commencement that segregate pure research and experimentation activities—such as computational fluid dynamics modeling, thermal barrier coating formulation, and hardware-in-the-loop failure testing—from routine post-qualification production or administrative support. Engineering project managers must contemporaneously log all test failures, rejected milestone submittals, and subsequent design iterations in a centralized configuration management database, directly cross-referencing those technical iterations to the cost accounting ledger to demonstrate that Aegis absorbed the unreimbursed rework costs against its fixed-price margin.
Case Study 2: Custom Enterprise Software & Industrial Robotics Engineering Firm (Commercial MSA & Statement of Work)
Scenario and Identified Legal Pitfalls

NexGen Automation & AI, Inc. ("NexGen"), a domestic industrial robotics and machine-vision software engineering firm, is engaged by a Fortune 500 pharmaceutical manufacturer ("PharmaCorp") under a Master Services Agreement (MSA) and a $12 million Fixed-Price Statement of Work (SOW) to design, engineer, and build a first-of-its-kind aseptic robotic inspection and high-speed vial-sorting system powered by custom edge-AI neural networks. NexGen faces three disqualifying legal traps identified in Lockheed Martin and subsequent Tax Court decisions (Tangel, MBJ, and Smith). First, Section 12 of PharmaCorp's standard procurement MSA states that all deliverables, inventions, software, designs, specifications, and work product conceived or developed by NexGen under any SOW shall be "works made for hire" and the sole and exclusive property of PharmaCorp, assigns all right, title, and interest therein to PharmaCorp, and designates all information, designs, and data generated thereunder as PharmaCorp Confidential Information that NexGen may not use, reproduce, or disclose for any purpose other than performing services for PharmaCorp without PharmaCorp's prior written consent. Under Lockheed Martin (as applied in Tangel and Smith), this clause strips NexGen of all "substantial rights," reducing its acquired engineering knowledge to non-qualifying "incidental benefits". Second, a commercial side letter stipulates that if NexGen wishes to incorporate the aseptic robotic gripper design into systems built for other medical device companies, NexGen must obtain a commercial license from PharmaCorp and pay a 5 percent royalty on gross sales, directly triggering the pay-to-use disqualification of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i). Third, although the SOW has a $12 million fixed price, the payment schedule calls for 12 equal monthly installments of $1 million payable within 30 days of invoice based on project schedule progression, and the termination-for-convenience clause entitles NexGen to payment for all work performed and hours expended up to the date of termination. Under Fairchild, Geosyntec, MBJ, and Grigsby (applying the funded-research framework described in Lockheed Martin, which itself did not decide the payment-contingency issue), invoice-based payments tied to general design services without a technical-success contingency render the research 100 percent funded.
Step 1: Contractual Restructuring & IP Carve-Outs (Rescuing "Substantial Rights" Under Commercial MSAs)

Commercial clients like PharmaCorp legitimately demand exclusivity over their proprietary pharmaceutical product formulas and specific factory floor configurations, but rarely need to prohibit an engineering vendor from reusing underlying robotics kinematics or AI architecture research. NexGen's tax and legal counsel must execute an Amended and Restated IP and Confidentiality Addendum before commencing work that bifurcates "Client-Specific Deliverables" from "Developer Research Results and Foreground Technology," modeling the allocation on the Lockheed Martin and Populous Holdings standards. Section 12.1 of the amended MSA should provide that upon final acceptance and full payment, PharmaCorp shall own the physical robotic workcell delivered under the SOW and the specific application-layer configuration files uniquely tailored to PharmaCorp's proprietary pharmaceutical compounds ("Client Deliverables"). Section 12.2 must then expressly state that notwithstanding Section 12.1 or any confidentiality provision to the contrary, NexGen retains the perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, non-exclusive, paid-up, and royalty-free right to make, use, reproduce, modify, and exploit all research results, engineering principles, kinematic designs, machine-vision training architectures, neural-network weight optimization techniques, source code libraries, and technical discoveries conceived, developed, or reduced to practice during the performance of the Agreement ("Research Results") in NexGen's trade or business, including in the design, manufacture, and sale of products or systems for other customers, without any requirement to obtain consent from, or pay any fee or royalty to, PharmaCorp.

Simultaneously, NexGen must rescind the side letter requiring it to pay a 5 percent royalty to use the robotic gripper design. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i) and Lockheed Martin, having to pay the client for the right to use the results of the research is an automatic disqualifier. To protect PharmaCorp's competitive posture without violating Section 41, the parties should replace the royalty clause with a narrow Field-of-Use Covenant whereby PharmaCorp receives an exclusive license to the specific vial-gripper geometry strictly within the narrow commercial field of injectable oncology biologics, while NexGen retains full title and the unencumbered, royalty-free right to make and use the research results and gripper technology across all other pharmaceutical, medical device, industrial, and commercial applications. Furthermore, to prevent a Tangel defect, the Confidentiality clause must be amended to state explicitly that PharmaCorp Confidential Information applies solely to preexisting technical and business information furnished by PharmaCorp to NexGen, and does not include or restrict NexGen's independent use of the Research Results generated by NexGen in performing the engineering and experimentation under the Agreement.
Step 2: Financial Risk & Payment Contingency Engineering (Transforming Invoice Billing into Technical-Success Contingency)

To ensure that NexGen's $12 million fixed-price SOW satisfies the first prong of the funded research test under Fairchild, Lockheed Martin, Grigsby, and MBJ, NexGen must eliminate the time-based monthly invoicing structure and tether all payments strictly to the technical success of the research. Rather than billing 12 equal monthly installments for design services, the SOW payment schedule must be restructured into four performance-gated technical milestones: Milestone 1 (20 percent payment), conditioned upon successful laboratory demonstration of sub-millimeter edge-AI optical defect detection at 600 vials per minute with a false-reject rate below (Factory Acceptance Test 1 — Vision Algorithm); Milestone 2 (30 percent payment), conditioned upon successful kinematic integration and zero-particulate generation verification of the high-speed robotic gripper in an ISO Class 5 cleanroom simulation (Factory Acceptance Test 2 — Electromechanical Prototype); Milestone 3 (30 percent payment), conditioned upon a full integrated system Factory Acceptance Test (FAT) demonstrating continuous 72-hour autonomous operation meeting all 450 quantitative technical specifications in Appendix A of the SOW; and Milestone 4 (20 percent payment), conditioned upon final Site Acceptance Testing (SAT) and formal written acceptance at PharmaCorp's facility.

To cement the financial risk allocation, the SOW must incorporate an explicit "Contingency of Payment on Technical Success" clause stipulating that all payments under the SOW are expressly contingent upon the technical success of NexGen's engineering research and the resulting system's satisfaction of the quantitative performance specifications set forth in Appendix A. The clause must grant PharmaCorp the affirmative right to inspect, evaluate, test, and reject any Milestone deliverable that fails to meet those technical specifications. In the event of technical failure or rejection, the contract must specify that PharmaCorp has no obligation to pay the Milestone fee, that NexGen is obligated at its sole cost and expense to re-engineer, modify, and re-test the system until technical compliance is achieved, and that if NexGen is unable to overcome the technical uncertainties to achieve final SAT acceptance, PharmaCorp may terminate the SOW for default and demand a full refund of all prior Milestone advances within 30 days. Additionally, the termination-for-convenience clause must be revised so that NexGen is compensated only for completed and technically accepted milestones prior to termination, eliminating any right to be reimbursed on a time-and-materials or quantum meruit basis for unaccepted, in-process research.
Step 3: Project Governance, Experimentation Tracking & Audit-Ready Substantiation

To ensure full compliance with I.R.C. § 41(d) and § 6001 record-keeping mandates and foreclose any variance challenge under I.R.C. § 7422(a), NexGen must implement rigorous contemporaneous documentation protocols at project inception. Prior to incurring project costs, NexGen's Lead Principal Engineer must author a formal Technical Uncertainty and Experimentation Charter identifying each separate business component—specifically the Edge-AI Vision Inference Engine, the Zero-Particulate Magnetic Levitation Gripper, and the Real-Time PLC Motion Controller—and documenting why existing commercial off-the-shelf capabilities cannot achieve the required 600-vial-per-minute ISO Class 5 performance targets. Throughout the development cycle, NexGen must integrate its Jira software development repositories and SolidWorks CAD revision logs with its labor time-tracking system so that every engineer's hours are contemporaneously tagged to specific hypothesis tests, simulation runs, prototype builds, and FAT/SAT validation trials. Finally, prior to filing its original Form 1120 (or any amended Form 1120X), NexGen must assemble a complete, self-contained substantiation binder ("Green Book") containing the executed MSA, SOW, and IP Addendum, the quantitative Appendix A specifications, the signed FAT/SAT acceptance certificates, the iterative failure and rework logs, and the exact employee-by-employee W-2 wage and prototype supply ledgers tied to each business component, ensuring that the administrative record is exhaustive and immune to both a Lockheed Martin factual variance challenge and a substantive funded-research disallowance.
Summary Matrix of Remedial Restructuring Across Both Case Studies

headers: Post-Remediation Structure Compliant with Lockheed Martin (210 F.3d 1366)

cells: Administrative Claim & Audit Substantiation (I.R.C. § 7422(a); Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2)
Filing Form 1120X with top-level divisional estimates while deferring contract-level cost accounting until post-audit or post-complaint discovery.
Full pre-filing ERP extraction and assembly of contract-by-contract "Green Books" mapping wages, supplies, and 65% subcontractor costs to specific business components prior to filing Form 1120/1120X.
IP Ownership & Usage Rights (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(2); Treas. Reg. § 1.41-2(a)(3))
"Work made for hire" assignment of all designs and data, coupled with NDA clauses barring contractor reuse without client's prior written consent.

Express retention of title to Subject Inventions (FAR 52.227-11) or explicit commercial carve-out preserving contractor's perpetual, non-exclusive, royalty-free right to use all Research Results in its trade or business without client consent.
Recoupment & Royalty Provisions (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(3)(i))
Requirement to pay client a 5% commercial licensing royalty to reuse designs, or ambiguous government cost recoupment language.

Elimination of royalties on internal/commercial use of research results; restriction of cost recoupment solely to third-party sales of identical military hardware; use of narrow Field-of-Use covenants for commercial clients.
Sovereign Export & Security Restrictions (ITAR / AECA)
Integration of ITAR export limits and security classification restrictions within the contract's IP rights ownership clauses.
Segregation of ITAR/AECA and security classification rules into a standalone regulatory compliance section acknowledging them solely as external requirements of sovereign law.
Payment Contingency & Financial Risk (Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4A(d)(1))
Unconditional monthly progress payments or time-based installment invoices; termination clauses reimbursing all incurred hours/costs.

Milestone payments or progress-payment liquidations strictly conditioned on formal technical inspection, testing, and acceptance against quantitative specifications, with mandatory self-funded cure and full refund obligations upon technical failure.

metaDescription: Lockheed Martin v. United States (Fed. Cir. 2000): a free non-exclusive right to use research results is a substantial right defeating funded research.
